{{Short description|Species of theropod dinosaurs}} {{Use mdy dates|date=February 2026}} {{Speciesbox | fossil_range = [[Late Cretaceous]] ([[Cenomanian]]), ~{{fossilrange|95}} | image = Spinosaurid MNBH EGA1.jpg | image_caption = Maxilla of the ''S. mirabilis'' holotype | display_parents = 2 | genus = Spinosaurus | species = mirabilis | authority = [[Paul Sereno|Sereno]] et al., [[2026 in archosaur paleontology|2026]] }} '''''Spinosaurus mirabilis''''' is a large [[extinct]] species of the [[spinosaurid]] theropod dinosaur [[genus]] ''[[Spinosaurus]]'', known from the [[Late Cretaceous]] [[Farak Formation]] of Niger. The species was named and described in 2026, based on various cranial and postcranial bones collected in two localities. It is characterized by a long, low snout, a [[scimitar]]-shaped midline crest on the top of the skull, and a large sail over the back. == Discovery and naming == {{Location map many|Niger | width = 225px | float = left | relief = yes | label = Iguidi | pos = bottom | coordinates={{coord|17|56|N|5|37|E|display=inline}} | label2 = Jenguebi | pos2 = right | coordinates2={{coord|16|40|N|10|15|E|display=inline}} | caption=Localities in Niger from which ''S. mirabilis'' is known |pushpin_relief=1 }} Fossils of ''Spinosaurus mirabilis'' were collected from outcrops of the [[Farak Formation]] of Niger during a series of excavations in 2000, 2019, and 2022, led by paleontologist [[Paul Sereno]]. Material was collected from two localities, Iguidi and Jenguebi. Most of the material comes from the latter, including the [[holotype]] specimen, [[Accession number (cultural property)|accessioned]] as MNBH JEN1, which comprises a fragmentary skull (right {{dinogloss|premaxilla}}, both {{dinogloss|maxillae}}, {{dinogloss|nasal}} crest, part of the right {{dinogloss|dentary}}, and five maxillary teeth). A second Jenguebi specimen, MNBH JEN2, includes part of a left maxilla, a nasal crest, fragments of the {{dinogloss|cervicals|cervical}} (neck) and {{dinogloss|dorsals|dorsal}} (back) vertebrae, part of the left {{dinogloss|ischium}}, and part of the left {{dinogloss|femur}}. Other specimens from this locality, MNBH JEN3–9, include a left maxilla, isolated teeth, another partial nasal crest, a right dentary, partial dorsal and {{dinogloss|caudals|caudal}} (tail) vertebrae, a partial {{dinogloss|chevron}}, a left {{dinogloss|tibia}}, and pedal {{dinogloss|phalanges}} (toe bones). Material from Iguidi, MNBH IGU11, 25, and 38–40, includes many isolated tooth crowns, fragments of the dorsal vertebrae, part of a caudal vertebra, and a single toe bone. As of its 2026 description, the Iguidi material is temporarily on loan to Sereno's Fossil Lab at the [[University of Chicago]], while all other specimens, including the holotype, are held at [[Abdou Moumouni University]] in Niger. MNBH IGU11, an anterior dorsal {{dinogloss|centrum}}, was initially identified as a mid-cervical centrum and referred to the coeval [[carcharodontosaurid]] ''[[Carcharodontosaurus iguidensis]]'' due to its similarities to cervical vertebrae erroneously referred to ''C. saharicus'', which actually come from a spinosaurid. This dorsal centrum was later thought to belong to ''[[Sigilmassasaurus]]'' or an indeterminate species of ''Spinosaurus'' until the description of ''S. mirabilis'' referred it to the species. In 2022, Sereno and colleagues identified MNBH JEN1 and MNBH JEN2 (then under the specimen numbers MNBH EGA1 and MNBH EGA2, respectively) as belonging to an indeterminate species of ''Spinosaurus''. In 2026, Sereno and colleagues [[Species description|described]] ''Spinosaurus mirabilis'' as a new species of the genus ''Spinosaurus'' based on these fossil remains. The [[Specific name (zoology)|specific name]], ''mirabilis'', is a [[Latin]] word meaning {{gloss|astonishing}}, alluding to the remarkably enlarged nasal-prefrontal crest that characterizes the species. Sereno and colleagues gave the species the nickname "hell heron".{{Cite web |last=Newcomb |first=Tim |date=2026-03-02 |title=Paleontologists Discovered a New 40-Foot-Long Dino Species. They Call It the 'Hell Heron.' |url=https://www.popularmechanics.com/science/archaeology/a70437513/new-spinosaurus-species/ |access-date=2026-03-04 |website=[[Popular Mechanics]]}} == Description == [[File:Spinosaurus mirabilis (MNBH IGU11, dorsal centrum).jpg|thumb|MNBH IGU11, a dorsal vertebral centrum referred to ''S. mirabilis'']] As expected, the skeletal anatomy of ''Spinosaurus mirabilis'' is similar to ''S. aegyptiacus'', the [[type species]] of the genus. It is only known from immature specimens, so the full size of this species when mature is uncertain. The holotype specimen, which belongs to a subadult individual, was estimated to have a full body length of around {{convert|8|m|ft}}. This is about 15% smaller than FSAC-KK-11888, the proposed [[neotype]] of ''S. aegyptiacus'', and about 61% the size of MSMN V4047 (a partial snout), one of the largest ''S. aegyptiacus'' specimens. A [[diastema]] (gap between the teeth) is present in the upper jaw to accommodate three of the large lower jaw teeth. The end of the snout in ''S. mirabilis'' differs from ''S. aegyptiacus'' in its slightly more arched [[premaxilla]] that rises above the rest of the snout, and subquadrate-shaped expansion of the anterior dentary, compared to the rounder morphology in ''S. aegyptiacus''. Specimen MNBH JEN4, which preserves a dentary and tibia, suggests the hindlimbs of ''S. mirabilis'' may be slightly proportionally longer than ''S. aegyptiacus''. The morphology of the preserved dorsal vertebrae implies the presence of a trunk sail formed by greatly elongated {{dinogloss|neural spines}}, although the shape of this sail is unknown. [[Autapomorphies]] (unique derived traits) identified in ''S. mirabilis'' include the proportionately low snout compared to other spinosaurids, with the [[Anatomical terms of location#Dorsal and ventral|dorsal and ventral]] margins parallel when seen from the side. The spacing of the rear maxillary teeth is also greater than in ''S. aegyptiacus''. One of the most unique traits of ''S. mirabilis'' is its distinctive pointed crest with a superficial [[scimitar]]-shape, formed by the {{dinogloss|nasal}} and {{dinogloss|prefrontal}} bones. This crest curves posterodorsally (upward and toward the rear). A network of vessels, in addition to longitudinal and crisscrossing striations and grooves, covers this crest, comparable to the condition seen in modern birds with bony crests, such as [[cassowaries]], the [[helmeted guinea fowl]], and the [[maleo]]. In these animals, the bone is encased in a [[keratinous]] sheath that significantly expands its size. In addition to the prominent dorsal (back) and caudal (tail) sails, the cranial crest likely functioned primarily for visual communication and display. == Classification == [[File:Spinosaurus mirabilis.png|thumb|Speculative [[paleoart|life restoration]]]] To test the relationships and affinities of ''Spinosaurus mirabilis'', Sereno and colleagues included it in an updated version of the [[phylogenetic]] matrix published by Sereno et al. (2022).{{cite journal |last1=Sereno |first1=Paul C. |last2=Myhrvold |first2=Nathan |last3=Henderson |first3=Donald M. |last4=Fish |first4=Frank E. |last5=Vidal |first5=Daniel |last6=Baumgart |first6=Stephanie L. |last7=Keillor |first7=Tyler M. |last8=Formoso |first8=Kiersten K. |last9=Conroy |first9=Lauren L. |year=2022 |title=''Spinosaurus'' is not an aquatic dinosaur |journal=[[eLife]] |volume=11 |pmid=36448670 |pmc=9711522 |article-number=e80092 |doi=10.7554/eLife.80092 |doi-access=free }} They consistently recovered the Nigerian taxon as the [[sister group]] to the better-known ''Spinosaurus aegyptiacus'', supporting their assignment to the same genus. representing a Cenomanian-aged fluvial system.{{cite book |last1=LeBlanc |first1=Jacques |title=Stratigraphic Lexicon: The Sedimentary Formations of The Republic of Niger, Africa |date=2022
